keycloak-37429.issue: Wrong locale script: The new `totpStep1` value uses Traditional Chinese characters and Taiwan-style vocabulary (手機, 應用程式) in the `messages_zh_CN.properties` file, which is the Simplified Chinese locale. Users of the zh_CN locale will see mixed-script text; the Simplified equivalent would be e.g. 在您的手机上安装以下应用程序之一：. Note the neighboring lines (totpStep2, totpStep3) remain in Simplified Chinese, making the inconsistency visible on the same screen.

Wrong Language: The Lithuanian `totpStep1` message was replaced with Italian text ("Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:"). Lithuanian users of the base account theme will see an Italian instruction for setting up an OTP authenticator. It should be translated to Lithuanian, e.g. "Įdiekite vieną iš šių programų savo mobiliajame telefone:", consistent with the other Lithuanian messages in this file and with how the same key was updated in the other locales (sv, sk, fi, zh_CN).

Wrong language translation: The `loginTotpStep1` value was replaced with Italian text ("Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:") in the Lithuanian (`messages_lt.properties`) message bundle. Lithuanian users will see an Italian instruction on the login page. The original Lithuanian sentence (which also carried the FreeOTP/Google Play links that other locales still keep, or at least a Lithuanian equivalent of the new wording) should be restored.

Unsupported MessageFormat syntax: The new value uses the Java-only `choice` format: `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}`. The admin-ui frontend renders these messages with a JavaScript ICU MessageFormat implementation (FormatJS/react-intl), which does not support the `choice` argument type (it uses `plural`/`select` instead). When this message is rendered in the admin console, formatting may fail or display the raw pattern instead of the intended text. Note the previous value in this JS file used doubled braces (`{{0}}`), consistent with the JS message-format conventions, while the Java-side theme files (themes/.../messages_en.properties) correctly use single braces with `choice`. The same pattern was also applied in js/apps/account-ui/.../messages_en.properties. Consider verifying how the admin-ui parses this key, or using a JS-compatible plural construct.

sentry-95633.issue: Failed messages are committed (data loss): In `thread-queue-parallel` mode, `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` wires `commit_offsets` into `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. In the queue consumer, a worker that raises inside `result_processor` logs the exception and then marks the offset complete in the `finally` block, so the offset becomes committable and `commit_offsets` advances past it. A message whose processing failed is therefore permanently skipped (offset committed, result never handled), unlike the serial path where an exception propagates and blocks the commit. If at-least-once delivery is intended, failed items need to be retried or left outstanding rather than marked complete.

Batching options silently ignored: In `thread-queue-parallel` mode, `max_batch_size` and `max_batch_time` are accepted but have no effect: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` submits each decoded message to the queue pool individually, with no batch collection. Operators configuring these knobs for this mode get per-message processing with no warning, which can materially change throughput and DB write patterns compared to the other parallel modes.

Threads spawned eagerly in constructor: `FixedQueuePool` (and its worker threads) is created in `__init__` with `num_queues=max_workers or 20`, before any strategy is built or any message consumed. Constructing a factory in `thread-queue-parallel` mode immediately starts 20 daemon threads even if `create_with_partitions` is never called (e.g., in tests or dry-run paths), and the default of 20 applies silently when `max_workers` is not provided. Consider lazily creating the pool in `create_with_partitions` and/or requiring an explicit queue count.

Data loss on processing failure: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, the `finally` block calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` unconditionally, including when `result_processor` raised an exception. The exception is only logged, so the offset is marked complete and the commit loop will happily commit past it, meaning a message whose processing failed is permanently skipped (at-least-once semantics are broken). This directly contradicts the class docstring "Only commits offsets after successful processing" and the PR's own `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` test, which asserts no commit happens after a processing failure — that test should fail against this implementation. Failed offsets should be left outstanding (or routed to a DLQ) instead of completed.

Silent message drop on submit errors: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, any exception from `decoder` or `grouping_fn` is caught and the offset is immediately added and completed, so the message is silently skipped and its offset becomes committable. A transient error (e.g., a codec/decoding hiccup, DB error inside `build_payload_grouping_key`) results in permanent data loss with only a log line. If dropping poison messages is intentional, it should be limited to decode failures and surfaced with a metric, not blanket `except Exception`.

Python version compatibility: `queue.Queue.shutdown()` (used in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` and relied on for `queue.ShutDown` in the worker) was only added in Python 3.13. If this codebase still supports 3.12, shutdown will raise `AttributeError` and workers will hang on `work_queue.get()` forever (they are daemon threads, so the process can still exit, but graceful drain is impossible). Verify the minimum supported Python version before merging.

join() calls close(): `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join()` calls `self.close()`. In arroyo's `ProcessingStrategy` contract, `join()` is only called after `close()`/`terminate()` by the framework, so this triggers a second shutdown of the queue pool and commit thread. `q.shutdown()` on an already-shut-down queue and `commit_thread.join()` on a finished thread are mostly harmless here (exceptions are swallowed), but it also means `join()` performs teardown the framework doesn't expect, and `terminate()` never joins the commit thread, leaving it to exit via the 1-second poll. Prefer making `join()` a no-op (or just wait) and keeping teardown in `close()`/`terminate()`.

Flaky assertion: `test_different_groups_distributed` asserts that 20 group keys hash to exactly 3 distinct queue indices. Queue assignment uses `hash(group_key) % num_queues`, and Python string hashing is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so there is no guarantee that 20 arbitrary keys cover all 3 queues. On an unlucky seed only 2 queues may be hit, making this test fail intermittently in CI. Consider seeding the hash, using a deterministic assignment check, or asserting a weaker property (e.g., more than one queue used).

Race condition in test: In `test_stats_reporting`, immediately after submitting 10 items the test asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0`. The worker threads run concurrently and can drain all queues before this line executes, making the assertion fail intermittently. The subsequent wait on `process_complete_event` already validates processing, so this eager assertion adds flakiness without additional coverage.

Test contradicts implementation: In `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling`, the test asserts that no offsets are committed when processing fails (`assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`). However, in the implementation the worker's `finally` block calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset()` even when `result_processor` raises, so failed offsets become committable and the commit loop will commit them. This means the assertion will fail (or only pass by timing luck if the 1-second commit loop hasn't fired before the assertion runs), making the test flaky at best and wrong at worst. The test should assert the actual intended behavior — either that failed offsets are still committed (matching the implementation) or the implementation should be changed to not complete offsets on failure.

Private API usage: The Kafka integration test drives `StreamProcessor` via its private methods `processor._run_once()` and `processor._shutdown()` instead of the public `run()`/`shutdown()` interface. This couples the test to arroyo internals and will break silently if arroyo changes these internals; it also bypasses normal signal handling and consumer lifecycle paths the production code exercises.

Timing-based flakiness: The new thread-queue-parallel tests rely on fixed sleep/poll loops (e.g. `max_wait = 20`/`50` iterations with `time.sleep(0.1)`) rather than events or deterministic synchronization. Under slow CI machines the commit loop (which fires every 1 second) may not have run before assertions like `assert test_partition in committed_offsets` execute, producing intermittent failures. Prefer waiting on an explicit signal (e.g. a commit-callback event) instead of polling `queue_pool.get_stats()`.

calcom-22532.issue: Wrong table updated / misleading status: The new call `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` bumps `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`, but the cache status surfaced by this PR (via `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` in `connectedCalendars.handler.ts`) is read from the `CalendarCache` table's `updatedAt`, not from `SelectedCalendar`. So this write does not affect the "Cache Status / Last updated" value shown to users. Additionally, it executes unconditionally after the cache-refresh block — including when availability was served from a still-valid cache — so it performs a write-many across all selected calendars for the credential on every availability fetch, adding DB load without achieving the stated intent. If the goal was to reflect cache freshness, the `CalendarCache` record's `updatedAt` (already maintained via `@updatedAt` in the schema) is the relevant field, and no explicit touch of `SelectedCalendar` is needed here.

Undeclared dependency: The `dev:cron` script now runs `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`, but `tsx` is not declared in `package.json` dependencies (and `ts-node` appears to have been dropped). `npx` will resolve `tsx` from node_modules if hoisted there by another workspace package, but if it isn't, the script will download an unpinned version from the registry at runtime — introducing version drift and a network dependency for a dev script. Safer to add `tsx` as a devDependency and invoke it directly (e.g., `tsx cron-tester.ts` or `yarn tsx`).

No-op update: `updateManyByCredentialId` is called from `CalendarService.ts` with an empty data object (`{}`) with the comment that it updates `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`. However, an empty `data` payload updates no fields, so the call is a no-op (and Prisma may raise a validation error for empty update data). Additionally, this PR adds `@updatedAt` only to the `CalendarCache` model in `schema.prisma`, not to `SelectedCalendar`, so even a non-empty update would not auto-refresh `updatedAt` unless the caller explicitly sets it. The cache-status feature that relies on this timestamp will not behave as intended.

Unconditional extra DB query: The handler now always instantiates `CalendarCacheRepository` and calls `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` on every `connectedCalendars` fetch, even when `connectedCalendars` is empty or contains no cacheable (e.g., Google) credentials. This adds an extra Prisma `groupBy` round-trip to a frequently-called endpoint for all users regardless of whether the result can ever be non-empty. Consider skipping the query when `credentialIds` is empty, or only enriching credentials whose integration actually uses the calendar cache.

Portability Bug: `sed -i '' -E ...` uses the macOS/BSD syntax for in-place editing. On GNU/Linux, `sed -i ''` treats the empty string as an input filename and fails with "sed: can't read : No such file or directory", so `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` is never updated on Linux machines. Use a portable form (e.g., `sed -i.bak` or detect the OS) or document macOS-only usage.

Stale URL Reuse: When Tunnelmole is already running, the script extracts the URL from `/tmp/tmole.log` without verifying the log exists or that the URL belongs to the current tunnel session. If the log file is missing (e.g., rebooted machine with tmole still running, or log from a previous session that was never cleaned), `TUNNEL_URL` will be empty and the script exits with "Failed to extract Tunnelmole URL" even though the tunnel is healthy; conversely, a stale log could yield a URL from an old, dead tunnel. Consider asking tmole for its current URL or validating the log's freshness.

Relative Env Path: `ENV_FILE="../.env"` is resolved relative to the caller's current working directory, not the script's location. Running the script from anywhere other than `scripts/` silently creates or edits a `.env` in the wrong directory (the script even `touch`es a new file if it's missing, masking the mistake). Use `ENV_FILE="$(dirname "$0")/../.env"` to anchor it to the script location.

Stale cache status after delete: Unlike `disconnectMutation`, which invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `viewer.apps.integrations` in `onSettled`, `deleteCacheMutation` performs no cache invalidation. It only calls the optional `onSuccess?.()` callback. When the component is rendered without an `onSuccess` prop (it is optional in the interface), deleting the cached data leaves the dropdown showing the old "Last updated" timestamp until an unrelated refetch happens, making the delete appear to have failed.

Hardcoded locale: `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)` hardcodes the `en-US` locale for formatting the cache timestamp, while the rest of the component uses `useLocale()` for i18n. Users in other locales will see dates formatted in US style (e.g., MM/DD/YY) next to translated UI text. Passing the user's locale from `useLocale()` would keep formatting consistent.

grafana-80329.issue: Unrelated behavior change: The cleanup job ticker interval is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is unrelated to the PR's stated goal (splitting annotation cleanup queries to avoid MySQL deadlocks) and significantly increases how often the cleanup job runs against the database. If intentional, it should be documented in the PR description; if not, it may cause unnecessary DB load, especially since the new annotation cleanup logic runs multiple batched queries per invocation. Note that the new batched cleanup loop in the annotations store terminates when a batch deletes nothing, so this does not cause an infinite loop, but the frequency change deserves explicit confirmation.

Error-level logging of routine cleanup: The new cleanup paths log every batch at `Error` severity (e.g. `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ...)`, `r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", ...)`, and the equivalents for count-based and orphaned-tag cleanup). This is routine, expected work that runs on a recurring cleanup job, so it will flood error dashboards/alerting on every cycle even when nothing is wrong. These should be Debug-level. Additionally, each message logs the full list of fetched IDs (`"ids", ids`), which can be thousands of entries per batch and is very expensive to format and emit; and `"err", err` is logged when `err` is known to be nil at that point (it was checked and returned on earlier), so it always logs `err=nil`.

sentry-80168.issue: Unimplemented abstract methods: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler`, which declares abstract methods `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and `build_occurrence_and_event_data` (per the diff in `src/sentry/workflow_engine/processors/detector.py`). The class body is just `pass`, so instantiating it (e.g., when `Detector.detector_handler` constructs the handler for a detector whose grouptype slug resolves to this class) will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class ...`. The previous `DetectorHandler` subclass had no abstract methods to implement, so this change silently breaks any code path that uses this handler. Either implement the required methods or keep it raising a clear NotImplementedError intentionally.

Possible enum mismatch: `PriorityLevel(new_status)` assumes `DetectorPriorityLevel` and `sentry.types.group.PriorityLevel` share the same member values. If the two enums define different numeric values for the same conceptual level (e.g. HIGH), the occurrence will be created with an unintended priority, and a value with no counterpart in `PriorityLevel` would raise a ValueError mid-evaluation. Worth verifying the two enums are value-compatible before shipping.

sentry-80528.issue: Dead code / lost conversion: In `get_monitor_environment_context`, a copy of `monitor.config` is made and `schedule_type` is converted to its display value on the copy, but the copy is never used — the returned dict includes the raw `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead. As a result the `schedule_type` in the monitor context sent to Kafka remains the raw enum/int value rather than the human-readable display value, and the conversion work is silently discarded. Either return `config` in the dict or drop the copy/conversion block.

Docstring mismatch: The `get_failure_reason` docstring contains typos ("humam readible") and its third example ("A failed check-in was detected") does not match the actual singular output, which is one of "An error check-in was detected" / "A missed check-in was detected" / "A timeout check-in was detected" via `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP`. Minor, but the example is misleading for future maintainers.

grafana-76186.issue: Silent context loss on fallback: In `grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext`, when the type assertion to `*log.ConcreteLogger` fails, the method falls back to `d.New()`, which returns a logger carrying only the wrapper's own context and silently discards everything stored in the passed `ctx` (e.g., contextual attributes added by the new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware`). There is no logging or error signal, so callers get a logger that appears contextual but is not. If the assertion can realistically fail (e.g., the infra logger wraps or replaces the concrete logger in some configurations), request-scoped fields like `dsName`, `dsUID`, or `uname` would be dropped from log output. It is uncertain how often the assertion fails in practice, but the fallback path is silent and lossy either way.

Missing coverage for streams: The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware instruments QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth and CollectMetrics, but SubscribeStream, PublishStream and RunStream pass the context through unchanged. This mirrors the old MetricsMiddleware behavior (which also skipped stream endpoints), so it may be intentional, but it means any downstream consumer of the contextual logger (e.g. LoggerMiddleware via FromContext) will not see pluginId/dsName/uname attributes for streaming requests. If streaming request logging matters, these endpoints should be instrumented too; otherwise consider a comment stating streams are deliberately excluded. Also note this new middleware has no dedicated test file, unlike the metrics middleware it was extracted from.

Lost traceID field: The `traceID` field (previously extracted via `tracing.TraceIDFromContext`) was removed from the "Plugin Request Completed" log entry. The new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` (which now supplies pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, dsUID) does not add a traceID, and nothing else in the shown diff injects trace information into the contextual logger. Unless the tracing middleware or `log.FromContext` implicitly attaches the trace ID, correlating plugin data-egress logs with traces is no longer possible from the log line alone. Worth verifying that trace correlation is preserved elsewhere before merging.

grafana-103633.issue: Cache key collision: `userPermDenialCacheKey` concatenates `name` and `parent` with `_` separators without escaping. Two different (name, parent) pairs can produce the same key — e.g. name="a", parent="b_c" and name="a_b", parent="c" both yield `ns.perm_user_action_a_b_c`. Since this key drives a hard deny in `Check`, a collision would deny a user access to a resource they are otherwise allowed to use. Using a separator that cannot appear in resource names/UIDs (or hashing the components) avoids this.

Stale denial cache blocks new grants: The `permDenialCache` is checked before the permission cache and the database, and an entry is written after every full-check denial. If a user is denied access to a resource and then granted permission (e.g., role or permission added), subsequent `Check` calls short-circuit on the denial entry and return `Allowed: false` until `shortCacheTTL` expires — the newly granted permission has no effect even though the permission-cache fallback path was designed to pick up fresh grants (see the "Fallback to the database on outdated cache" test). There is no invalidation of denial entries when permissions change. If this staleness window is intentional, it should be documented; otherwise denial entries should be invalidated on permission changes or the denial check should be consulted only after the permission cache misses.

Swallowed errors in cache fast path: In `Check`, `getCachedIdentityPermissions` errors are ignored wholesale (`if err == nil`). This is fine for `cache.ErrNotFound`, but the function can also return real errors — e.g., a `GetUserIdentifiers` failure or `fmt.Errorf("unsupported identity type: %s", idType)`. In those cases the code silently falls through and repeats the same work via `getIdentityPermissions`, which will hit the same error, doubling the failure work and skipping the cache-usage metric semantics. Distinguishing `cache.ErrNotFound` from other errors (or at least logging non-not-found errors) would avoid masking real failures.

Duplicate cache lookups: When the permission cache misses in `Check`, `getCachedIdentityPermissions` runs (resolving user identifiers and checking `permCache`), then `getIdentityPermissions` runs and performs the identical identifier resolution and cache lookup again inside `getUserPermissions`. On every cache miss this doubles the identifier-resolution work. Minor performance concern, but it is on the hot path of every uncached check.

grafana-79265.issue: Missing coverage: The new test only covers the error path: when the device limit is reached and the incoming device does not already exist, `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. There is no test asserting the complementary behavior that an existing device (same `DeviceID`) can still be updated successfully when the limit is reached — which is the core promise of the `updateDevice` fallback path. A test creating one device, hitting the limit, then calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice` again with the same `DeviceID` and asserting no error (and that the row was updated) would guard against regressions where legitimate returning anonymous users are locked out.

Blocking request path: TagDevice was previously invoked in a background goroutine with its own timeout and panic recovery, so failures or slowness never affected the request. It is now called synchronously during Authenticate on every anonymous request, adding a DB round-trip (and, when the device limit is configured, an extra CountDevices query) to the authentication latency of each request. A slow or loaded database now directly delays all anonymous traffic, and there is no per-call timeout anymore since the request context is used. If this is intentional, consider documenting it; otherwise restore async tagging or add a timeout.

Error surfaced to anonymous users: When ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned, Authenticate now fails the whole authentication instead of falling back to anonymous access. Once the configured device limit is reached, every new anonymous visitor receives an authentication error (likely a failed request) rather than being served as anonymous with a default identity. If the intent is to cap tracked devices, it may be preferable to still return the anonymous identity and skip tagging. Flagging as a possible unintended UX/availability impact since the PR title suggests a tracking limit, not blocking access.

Behavior change in TagDevice: TagDevice previously always returned nil after logging a UI-tagging failure at Debug level; it now propagates the error from tagDeviceUI to its callers. The visible caller in client.go handles this (warns, or fails auth on ErrDeviceLimitReached), but any other existing callers of TagDevice that assumed it never returns an error will now see failures for transient DB errors during UI tagging. If skipping the early return is intentional, consider whether non-limit errors should still be swallowed here to preserve the old contract, since UI tagging is best-effort telemetry.

Race condition: The limit enforcement is a non-atomic check-then-act: `CountDevices` is read, then a new row is inserted with no locking or transaction spanning both steps. Under concurrent anonymous requests (common at scale, which is exactly when the limit matters), multiple requests can pass the count check simultaneously and insert extra rows, exceeding `deviceLimit`. The limit will be soft/approximate rather than hard. If a hard cap is required, the insert should be conditional (e.g., INSERT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(...)) < limit within a transaction).

calcom-22345.issue: Lost input validation: The constructor now accepts `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions`, a plain type where `teamId` is optional, instead of the zod-validated `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` where `teamId` is required for the "team" scope. A caller can now pass `{ scope: "team", userId, orgId }` with no `teamId` and it type-checks; `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` will then call `teamRepo.findByIdAndParentId({ id: undefined, ... })`, producing a query that matches nothing (or a runtime error depending on the repository) instead of being rejected at the boundary. The zod schema still exists but is no longer enforced by this class.

Possible Bug: `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition` and `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` still take `Extract<InsightsBookingServiceOptions, { scope: ... }>` while the constructor now accepts `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions`. Since `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` for scope "team" requires `teamId`, TypeScript will flag passing the public (optional-teamId) options into these private methods, and the two types can silently drift. The parameter types should be updated to the public options type (or a shared narrowed type) for consistency.

calcom-10967.issue: Logic Inversion: The refactor inverts the conditional logic rather than just changing syntax. Previously, `slug` was spread into the organization create payload when `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` was falsy (`...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })`), and `requestedSlug` was set in metadata when it was truthy. The new code spreads `slug` only when `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` is truthy and sets `requestedSlug` only when it is truthy. If the original behavior was intentional (slug stored directly on the organization only when billing is disabled, while always recording the requested slug in metadata when billing is enabled), this change silently flips which deployments persist the slug, potentially breaking organization lookup by slug in non-billing deployments. If the inversion is an intentional fix, it should be called out explicitly in the PR description and covered by a test, since no tests are included.

Wrong calendar selection for collective events: `createEvent` now always uses `destinationCalendar[0]` (the "main host" calendar) as the target calendar. Unlike the Google Calendar service in this same PR, which selects the destination calendar matching the executing `credentialId`, this service ignores which credential is running. In a collective event where multiple hosts' destination calendars are passed (as built in `handleNewBooking.ts`), the first entry may belong to a different user's credential than the one executing this service. The event would then be attempted in a calendar externalId that this credential may not own, resulting in a 404/403 from the Microsoft Graph API or the event being created on the wrong host's calendar. Consider matching the destination calendar by credentialId (as the Google implementation does) instead of blindly taking the first element.

Collective events limited to one calendar: The new code wraps only a single destination calendar (`booking.destinationCalendar || user.destinationCalendar`) into an array. For COLLECTIVE event types, `handleNewBooking.ts` now collects `teamDestinationCalendars` from all hosts and pushes them into `evt.destinationCalendar`, but the payment webhook path (both `getBooking` and `handlePaymentSuccess`) never does this. A paid collective booking will therefore only have its calendar event created on the organizer's (or booking's) calendar, and the other hosts' destination calendars are silently ignored. Consider deriving the full list the same way `handleNewBooking` does, or at least confirm this asymmetry is intentional.

Wrong calendar selected for collective events: This PR changes `destinationCalendar` to an array (one entry per host in collective events) and this service now always uses `destinationCalendar[0]`. The `Calendar` interface was updated so `createEvent` receives a `credentialId`, and the Google service uses it to find the destination calendar matching its own credential. The Lark service ignores the new `credentialId` parameter and blindly takes the first array element. In a collective booking where the first host uses a different calendar provider (e.g., Google) and a later host uses Lark, `createEvent`/`updateEvent`/`deleteEvent` will operate on the wrong host's calendar (or throw "no calendar id" behavior changes), creating or deleting the event in the incorrect calendar. Consider selecting the entry whose `credentialId` matches the credential passed to `createEvent`, or whose `integration` matches the Lark integration, as the Google service does.

Possible Bug: The new `externalId` parameter is echoed back verbatim in the returned `EventResult.externalId`, and `EventManager` now uses `result.externalId` to persist `externalCalendarId` on booking references. However, the actual calendar the event is created on is decided inside each calendar service, not here. For example, the Google service selects the calendar by matching `credentialId` and falls back to `"primary"` when no destination matches, and other services fall back to the default calendar when `externalId` is absent. In those fallback cases the event is created on a different calendar than the `externalId` reported here, so the booking reference will store an `externalCalendarId` that doesn't point at the real event, which can break later update/delete flows that rely on that reference.

Silent failure path: When `calendar.createEvent` rejects with a 404, the catch returns `undefined` while `success` is set to false, and the result is still returned with the new `externalId` and `credentialId` fields populated. Downstream code (e.g., `EventManager` building booking references from `result.externalId`/`result.credentialId`) may now record a calendar reference for an event that was never created, since the 404 path previously had no externalId/credentialId surfaced in the result. Worth verifying that callers distinguish `success: false` results before persisting references.

Possible Bug: In `updateEvent`, the fallback now does `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. When `externalCalendarId` is not provided (undefined), the `find` predicate compares `cal.externalId === undefined` and always fails, so `selectedCalendar` becomes `undefined` and the update is issued with an undefined `calendarId`. Previously the code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`, so the event was still updated on the correct calendar. Any caller that invokes `updateEvent` without an explicit `externalCalendarId` (which the optional parameter allows) will now target the wrong calendar or fail.

Possible Bug: Same pattern in `deleteEvent`: `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` returns `undefined` whenever `externalCalendarId` is undefined, so the delete no longer falls back to the event's destination calendar externalId as it did before. Deleting a booking whose calendar reference lacks `externalCalendarId` will pass an undefined `calendarId` to `calendar.events.delete`, causing the event to remain on the calendar (orphaned) or the call to error out.

Incomplete multi-reference handling: The PR's intent is to support multiple calendar references (collective events with multiple host destination calendars), and the outer loop was changed from `find` to `filter` to iterate all references. However, inside the recurring-event branch, the per-booking lookup still uses `updBooking.references.find((ref) => ref.type.includes("_calendar"))`, which only picks the first calendar reference for each remaining booking. For a recurring collective booking with multiple hosts, cancellation with `allRemainingBookings` will delete only the first host's calendar event and leave the other hosts' events on their calendars. The lookup should be `filter` (and iterate) to match the new multi-reference behavior.

Silent skip on missing credential: When a calendar reference has a `credentialId` but the credential is neither in `bookingToDelete.user.credentials` nor found in the DB via `prisma.credential.findUnique`, the reference is silently skipped — no log, no error, and the calendar event is never deleted. This is a new code path introduced by the DB fallback lookup; a stale/deleted credential (e.g., user disconnected the calendar app) now results in orphaned calendar events with no operator visibility. Consider logging when `calendarCredential` remains undefined after both lookups.

Possible Bug: `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` silently does nothing when `evt.destinationCalendar` is null. Since `destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists, a COLLECTIVE team event whose organizer has no destination calendar will silently drop all team members' destination calendars instead of creating the array. The team members' calendars then never receive the event. Use `(evt.destinationCalendar ??= []).push(...)` or equivalent.

Data not persisted: The booking record only connects `evt.destinationCalendar[0]` (the organizer's/eventType's calendar) via `connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id }`. The team destination calendars pushed into `evt.destinationCalendar` for COLLECTIVE events are used to create calendar events but are never connected to the booking row, so the booking's persisted `destinationCalendar` relation loses the other members' calendars. If downstream flows (reschedule, cancel) rely on the booking's destinationCalendar list, they will only see the first one. Worth confirming this is intentional.

Error masking: In `loadUsers`, the explicit `throw new Error("dynamicUserList is not properly defined or empty.")` (and the `eventType.hosts` check) is caught by the surrounding catch and converted into a generic 500 `HttpError({ message: "Unable to load users" })`, since a plain `Error` is neither `HttpError` nor a Prisma known request error. The specific validation message is lost and a client-input problem is reported as a server error; these should be thrown as `HttpError({ statusCode: 400 })` directly.

Possible Bug: The new code destructures `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` and then accesses `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without any null check. When `destinationCalendar` is `null` or an empty array (which is now a valid state per the PR — e.g. the webhook payload uses `destinationCalendar: []`), `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` and this line throws a TypeError, failing the whole event creation. The old code used optional chaining (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`) and handled this safely. A guard like `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"` is needed.

Lost externalCalendarId: `externalCalendarId` is now taken from `result.externalId`, but `result.externalId` is only populated when `createEvent(credential, event, destination.externalId)` is called with the destination's externalId. In the branch where a destination has no `credentialId` (the legacy path in `createAllCalendarEvents`), `createEvent` is called without an externalId, so `result.externalId` is `undefined` and the booking's calendar reference loses its `externalCalendarId` — previously it was copied from `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. This can break subsequent update/delete of the calendar event for bookings created via that path.

Possible Bug: In `updateCalendarEvent`, when a reference has a `credentialId` that is not found in `this.calendarCredentials`, the code fetches the credential from the DB, but only assigns it if `credentialFromDB.app?.slug` exists. If the DB lookup fails or the credential has no associated app (e.g. legacy credentials), `credential` remains `undefined` and `updateEvent(credential, ...)` is still called, which will throw inside the calendar service (or silently fail) instead of being skipped or reported. The same pattern exists in `createAllCalendarEvents`, where the event creation is silently skipped with no logging when the credential can't be resolved.

Credential fetch duplication: The identical ~25-line "fetch credential from DB and map to credential object" block is duplicated verbatim in `createAllCalendarEvents` and `updateCalendarEvent`. Extracting it into a shared helper would reduce the risk of the two copies drifting (one already requires `app?.slug` while the other silently skips). This is a maintainability concern rather than a functional bug.

calcom-10600.issue: Accessibility regression: Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the password visibility toggle button removes it from keyboard tab order. Keyboard-only users (and screen reader users relying on keyboard navigation) can no longer toggle password visibility, which is an accessibility regression for a shared UI component used across the app (e.g., the login and settings password fields). If the intent was to prevent focus stealing when clicking the toggle, a common alternative is `onMouseDown={(e) => e.preventDefault()}`, which keeps the button keyboard-accessible while avoiding focus shift.

Weak client-side validation: `minLength={10}` / `maxLength={11}` only bound the raw string length, so an 11-character input without a dash (e.g., "1234567890X") passes client validation but will never match a stored 10-character code after the backend strips dashes, producing a confusing "incorrect backup code" error. A regex pattern (e.g., `^\d{5}-?\d{5}$`) would match the actual code format. Low severity since the server still validates, but the client check gives a false sense of correctness.

Missing autoFocus prop: The sibling `TwoFactor` component was updated in this PR to accept an `autoFocus` prop so callers can control focus behavior (e.g., `DisableTwoFactorModal` passes `autoFocus={false}`), but `BackupCode` has no equivalent. When the disable modal toggles to the backup-code view, focus behavior will be inconsistent with the TOTP view. Minor UX inconsistency introduced by the same PR.

Backup codes silently invalidated: Every call to the setup endpoint overwrites `backupCodes` with a freshly generated set, even if the user never completes enabling 2FA (the handler also sets `twoFactorEnabled: false`). If a user starts setup, abandons it, and later re-runs setup (or another session/tab triggers it), any previously issued backup codes that the user may have saved or printed are silently invalidated with no warning. Consider only generating backup codes when none exist, or explicitly warning the user that re-running setup rotates their codes.

Unhandled JSON.parse: `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, ...))` is not wrapped in try/catch. If the stored `backupCodes` value is corrupted, was written by an older format, or decryption yields non-JSON output, this throws an unhandled exception and the client gets an opaque 500 instead of a meaningful error. The sibling login flow in `next-auth-options.ts` has the same pattern, but here the failure occurs on a settings/disable path where a clean error message is expected.

Unvalidated input type: `req.body.backupCode` is used directly without validating it is a string. Since the handler accepts an arbitrary JSON body, a client can send `{"backupCode": 123}` or an object; `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll` would then throw a TypeError, producing an unhandled 500. A `typeof req.body.backupCode === "string"` check (or zod validation) before use would prevent this.

Backup code not consumed: When disabling 2FA with a backup code, the matched code is verified but not marked as used at that point; the code relies on the final update setting `backupCodes: null` to invalidate them. This is safe only because disable always reaches that update — but note the comment "we delete all stored backup codes at the end" makes the correctness depend on control flow further down the handler. If any early return is ever added between verification and the final update, the code would remain valid. Low severity given current flow, but worth an explicit guard or consuming the code at verification time.

Weak assertion: The newly added FIXME comment confirms that the assertion `await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch]').isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` passes even when the switch is not checked, meaning this step of the test does not actually verify 2FA was enabled at that point. Since this test is the setup path that later exercises the new backup-code download/copy/close flow, a regression in enabling 2FA could go unnoticed while the backup-code assertions still pass. The sibling test below uses `[data-state="checked"]` and works correctly; this assertion should be updated to match.

Incomplete coverage: The new backup-code test block verifies the download filename and that a success toast appears on copy, but leaves explicit TODOs for checking the downloaded file content and clipboard content. As written, the copy test would pass even if the clipboard contains wrong or empty data (the toast is shown unconditionally by the UI), and the download test would pass even if the file content is malformed. Given backup codes are a security-recovery feature, at least one content assertion would meaningfully strengthen the test.

Unguarded JSON.parse: `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, ...))` is not wrapped in try/catch. If the stored `backupCodes` value is corrupt, was encrypted with a different/rotated `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, or is not a JSON array, this throws an unhandled exception during login. The user gets a generic InternalServerError and cannot authenticate even with a valid backup code, with no way to recover short of manual DB intervention. Consider catching the error and treating it as `MissingBackupCodes` so the user is directed to regenerate codes.

Non-constant-time comparison: `backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))` compares the user-supplied backup code with a plain string equality check, which is not constant-time. Backup codes are high-entropy (10 hex chars), so this is low practical risk, but since this is an authentication secret check, a timing-safe comparison (e.g., `crypto.timingSafeEqual`) would be more robust. Note the same pattern exists in the disable endpoint (reviewed separately).

Stuck in backup-code view: In the login response handler, `ErrorCode.SecondFactorRequired` only sets `twoFactorRequired(true)` but never resets `twoFactorLostAccess`. If the server returns this error while the user is in the "lost access" (backup code) view — e.g., the backup code field was submitted empty or the request reached the server without a backup code — the UI stays on the `BackupCode` input with no error message displayed, since the `errorMessage` branch for this code is not set. The user gets no feedback and cannot tell why login did not proceed. Consider resetting `twoFactorLostAccess(false)` (or showing an error) when this error code is received.

Form validation gap: A `backupCode` field was added to `LoginValues` and registered via the new `BackupCode` component, but the diff does not show `formSchema` being updated to include/validate `backupCode`. If the zod schema still only validates `email`/`password`/`totpCode`, an empty backup code can be submitted to the server (react-hook-form's HTML `required` on the TextField may not block submit since the form is driven by the zod resolver), resulting in a confusing server-side error instead of client-side validation. Please confirm the schema covers the new field.

Possible unintended submit: The new "Lost access" / "Go back" toggle button in `DialogFooter` has an `onClick` handler but no explicit `type="button"`. If this footer is rendered inside the `Form` element (as the sibling `EnableTwoFactorModal` suggests, where analogous buttons call `e.preventDefault()`), a click would also submit the form and trigger `handleDisable` with whatever values are currently filled in, in addition to toggling the view. Adding `type="button"` (as done for the copy/close buttons in `EnableTwoFactorModal`) avoids this. Flagging with some uncertainty since the exact DOM nesting of `DialogFooter` relative to `Form` is not fully visible in this diff.

Possible Bug: After a successful TOTP verification, `onEnable()` is no longer called immediately; it is deferred to the "close" button in the DisplayBackupCodes step. However, the Dialog's `onOpenChange` path (Escape key, clicking the overlay, or the dialog's close X) still closes the modal without calling `onEnable()` or `resetState()`. In that scenario 2FA is already enabled server-side, but the parent component is never notified (e.g., the two-factor switch in settings won't refresh), and the modal state (backup codes, password, step) is left stale — reopening the modal will show leftover backup codes from the previous session instead of starting fresh at ConfirmPassword.

Resource Leak: `resetState()` clears the password and step but does not revoke `backupCodesUrl` or clear `backupCodes`. Each call to `handleSetup` creates a new object URL (revoking only the previous one), but when the modal is closed/reset the last URL is never revoked, leaking a Blob URL containing the user's unencrypted backup codes for the lifetime of the page. The backup codes also remain in component state after the flow completes.

Type Safety: `useState([])` for `backupCodes` infers type `never[]`, so `setBackupCodes(body.backupCodes)` (any) bypasses type checking entirely. Typing it as `useState<string[]>([])` would catch malformed API responses at compile time rather than rendering `undefined` values that then crash `formatBackupCode` (`code.slice` on undefined).

calcom-8087.issue: Unawaited async forEach: Changing the `forEach` callback to `async` makes the callback return a promise that `forEach` ignores, so the calendar deletions (`calendar?.deleteEvent(...)`) become fire-and-forget. The surrounding `try` block cannot catch any rejection from these async operations, so a failed `getCalendar` or `deleteEvent` (e.g., network error or invalid credential) will result in an unhandled promise rejection and the calendar event may silently remain undeleted. Since `getCalendar` is now async, the previously synchronous flow is fully asynchronous and should be awaited, e.g. with a `for...of` loop or `Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))`.

Fire-and-forget async in forEach: The `forEach` callback is now `async`, so the promises returned by `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` and `deleteMeeting(...)` are not awaited by anyone. Two concrete consequences: (1) the surrounding `try`/`catch` cannot catch rejections from these operations — a failed calendar event deletion (e.g., expired OAuth token) becomes an unhandled promise rejection and the reschedule flow continues as if deletion succeeded; (2) callers of `Reschedule` get no signal when (or whether) the deletions complete. Since `bookingRefsFiltered` is a small array, a `for...of` loop with `await` (as done elsewhere in this PR, e.g. in `handleCancelBooking.ts`) would preserve error handling and sequencing.

Fire-and-forget async forEach: Changing the `forEach` callback to `async` means the returned promises from `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` and `deleteMeeting(...)` are not awaited or collected. The router procedure can complete (and respond) before any calendar event deletion actually finishes, so a client rescheduling a booking may see stale events, and any rejection inside the callback becomes an unhandled promise rejection with no way for the caller to learn the deletion failed. Since `getCalendar` is now async, the deletion calls only start after an await inside the callback, making the race more likely. Use a `for...of` loop with `await` (as done in `handleCancelBooking.ts` in this same PR) or collect promises with `Promise.all`.

Fire-and-forget async forEach: The callback passed to `.forEach(async (credential) => {...})` is now async because `getCalendar` became async. `forEach` does not await async callbacks, so the loop body (including the `for (const updBooking of updatedBookings)` loop and the calendar `deleteEvent` calls) runs detached from the surrounding async function: the handler can complete (and the response be sent) before any calendar deletion finishes, and any rejection inside the callback becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Previously the synchronous `getCalendar` meant the `deleteEvent` promises were at least created synchronously within the same tick. Consider collecting promises and awaiting them (e.g. `Promise.all` over a `map`), as was effectively done in the sibling `else` branch that was correctly converted to a `for...of` loop.
